## Analysis

**The blocking dependence:** The loop combines two operations on `u` and `v` in a single iteration:
- Line 6 writes to `u[ju[i]]` and reads from `v[kv[i]]`
- Line 7 reads from `u[ku[i]]` (which might have been written by line 6 in this or an earlier iteration) and writes to `v[jv[i]]`

The problem is **loop-carried anti/true dependences** on the indirection: iteration i might write to a location that iteration j (j > i) reads from via the indirect indices. DiscoPoP cannot prove these don't exist due to the scatter through `ju[]` and `kv[]`.

**Solution:** Split the loop into two passes:
1. First pass: all updates to `u` (reading old `v` values)
2. Second pass: all updates to `v` (reading new `u` values from pass 1)

This **moves the dependence** (all `u` writes happen before any `v` read-update that uses them) without deleting it. Each loop independently either has no loop-carried dependence (if indices don't alias) or becomes easier for DiscoPoP to characterize. The functional behavior is preserved because the synchronization between the two passes is now explicit.

---Done. The rewrite splits the loop into two sequential phases:

This decouples the anti-dependence (iteration i writing `u` before iteration i reading it in the same iteration). Each loop can now be independently parallelized if there are no aliasing conflicts within it—and DiscoPoP will verify this at profile time on the actual data.

The functional behavior is preserved: the implicit barrier between the loops ensures that all `u` updates seen by the second loop include the complete result of the first loop, maintaining the original read-after-write semantics.
